fields.Front: How do OO techniques view a software system?
fields.Back: As networks of communicating objects: each object is an instance of a class; all objects of a class share similar features (attributes and methods); classes can be specialized by subclasses; and objects communicate by sending messages, which in C++ means calling each other's methods.

fields.Front: List the five things an object may do in response to a message.
fields.Back: Update its internal state; return a value from its internal state; perform a calculation based on its state and return the calculated value; create a new object (or set of objects); delegate part or all of the task to some other object.

fields.Front: Which of the five message responses does AuditService::record illustrate?
fields.Back: The fifth, delegation: void record(const std::string& msg) { logger.log(msg); } forwards the whole task to another object and does nothing else itself.

fields.Text: UML stands for {{c1::Unified Modeling Language}}: a standard set of {{c1::notations}} for use in modeling object-oriented systems.
fields.Extra: The course encounters class diagrams, sequence/collaboration diagrams, state diagrams, and activity and use case diagrams. The project requires class, sequence, and use case diagrams, submitted as PDF.

fields.Text: The two design targets for every object: {{c1::highly cohesive}} (a single purpose, making use of all its features) and {{c1::loosely coupled}} (dependent on only a few other classes).
fields.Extra: This restates Week 1's 'high cohesion, low coupling' at the level of each class you draw.
